holdReason: Confidence ceiling: her documented public record is overwhelmingly about flight outcomes and records rather than personal working style, so most trait inferences sit at the 'strong_inference' tier rather than 'documented.' After two remediation passes (12 -> 20 scored attributes, coverage now comfortably clears 0.6), average confidence (0.501) still falls meaningfully short of the 0.55 floor; closing the remaining gap would require either implausibly many further additions or inflating existing entries past what the source material supports.

sources.title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum — Amelia Earhart

risk_tolerance.rationale: Undertook multiple long-distance solo and pioneering flights (the 1932 solo transatlantic crossing, the 1935 solo Hawaii-to-California flight) using period aviation technology with well-documented, substantial fatality rates among contemporaries attempting similar routes, culminating in her disappearance during the 1937 round-the-world attempt.

achievement_drive.rationale: Set a documented, sustained sequence of specific aviation distance/speed/altitude records across roughly a decade, corroborated via the Smithsonian's own record of her flight log and achievements.

independent_thinking.rationale: Pursued a professional aviation career at a time when the field was overwhelmingly closed to women, and co-founded the Ninety-Nines organization to support other women aviators, documented via the organization's own institutional history.

proactive_agency.rationale: Self-initiated and organized her own record-attempt flights, including securing sponsorship and technical support for the 1937 round-the-world attempt, documented via the well-recorded planning history of that flight.

leadership_drive.rationale: Co-founded and served as the first president of the Ninety-Nines, an organization for women pilots that persisted well beyond her own career, documented via the organization's institutional record.

discipline.rationale: Sustained a demanding schedule of flight training, record attempts, and public lecturing/writing to fund her aviation career across roughly a decade.

impact_motivation.rationale: Explicitly and repeatedly framed her flying achievements around expanding opportunities for women in aviation, documented via her own public writing and lectures, rather than personal record-seeking alone.

social_assertiveness.rationale: Sustained a substantial public speaking, writing, and media career alongside her flying, documented via her published books and extensive contemporary press coverage.

adaptability.rationale: Period aviation required real, sustained technical and situational adjustment to frequently changing aircraft and weather conditions, though the surviving record documents her achievements more than granular in-flight decision-making.

persistence.rationale: Continued pursuing increasingly ambitious flights after an earlier failed 1937 round-the-world attempt (a takeoff crash in Hawaii) rather than abandoning the project, documented via the well-recorded timeline of two separate 1937 attempts.

detail_orientation.rationale: Flight navigation and planning at this technological period required real precision, though the surviving public record documents her public achievements and advocacy more thoroughly than her specific technical working methods.

planning_orientation.rationale: The 1937 round-the-world attempt required extensive advance logistical planning (aircraft modification, fuel stops, navigator coordination), documented via the well-recorded preparation history of that flight.

curiosity.rationale: Engaged beyond flying itself in writing, public lecturing, and a practical clothing line she designed for active women, documented via her own business ventures and bibliography.

opportunity_sensing.rationale: Recognized and seized the 1928 opportunity to be the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air (initially as a passenger), leveraging the resulting publicity into her own independent solo flying career, documented via the well-recorded history of her career's origin.

competitiveness.rationale: Repeatedly pursued being specifically first or fastest on a given route (first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic, first person to solo Hawaii-to-California), documented via the Smithsonian's own framing of her record sequence as deliberately comparative achievements.

execution_speed.rationale: Several of her records were explicitly speed records over a fixed route, documented via the Smithsonian's flight-log data, though the surviving record documents outcomes more than her decision-making pace generally.

collaboration.rationale: The 1937 attempt required sustained coordination with navigator Fred Noonan and a ground logistics/sponsorship team, documented via the well-recorded planning history, though this reflects necessary operational partnership more than a broader collaborative disposition.

persuasiveness.rationale: Secured sponsorship, media contracts, and public backing for successive record attempts across her career, documented via the well-recorded commercial and promotional history of her flights.

cross_domain_range.rationale: Sustained parallel work across flying, public lecturing, and published writing (her books '20 Hrs., 40 Min.' and 'The Fun of It'), documented via her own bibliography.

mastery_orientation.rationale: Continued pursuing progressively more technically demanding flights (Atlantic solo, then Pacific solo, then round-the-world) across roughly a decade rather than repeating an early success.
